title: Adam Laurie
summary: British security researcher known by the alias "Major Malfunction," who co-discovered and publicized the Bluetooth "bluesnarfing" vulnerability in 2003 and later created the open-source RFIDIOt and RFIDler RFID/NFC security research tools.

title: Adrian Lamo: The 'Homeless Hacker'
summary: The complex and controversial story of Adrian Lamo, a gray-hat hacker known for his high-profile intrusions and his role in reporting Chelsea Manning.

title: Alex Rice
summary: Alex Rice is a co-founder and the Chief Technology Officer (and Chief Information Security Officer) of HackerOne, the vulnerability coordination and bug bounty platform he helped launch in 2012 after leading product security at Facebook.

title: Alex Stamos
summary: Alex Stamos is an American cybersecurity researcher and executive who, as Facebook's Chief Security Officer, led the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election, and later founded the Stanford Internet Observatory to study online disinformation and platform abuse.

title: Andres Riancho
summary: Andres Riancho is an Argentine application-security researcher and open-source developer, based in Buenos Aires, best known for creating w3af (Web Application Attack and Audit Framework), a widely used open-source web vulnerability scanner and exploitation tool.

title: Barnaby Jack
summary: Barnaby Jack was a New Zealand-born security researcher best known for publicly demonstrating that ATMs could be forced to dispense cash on command ('jackpotting') and for pioneering research into vulnerabilities in wireless insulin pumps and implantable cardiac devices, work that helped establish medical device security as a distinct field before his sudden death in 2013.

title: Brian Krebs
summary: Brian Krebs is an American investigative journalist who became one of the most influential chroniclers of cybercrime, breaking major stories such as the 2013 Target data breach and, through his deep sourcing in underground carding and cybercrime forums, turning his independent blog KrebsOnSecurity into a top-tier source on the cybercriminal underground.

title: Bruce Schneier
summary: Bruce Schneier is an American cryptographer, computer security professional, and writer whose Blowfish and Twofish ciphers, best-selling books, and long-running Crypto-Gram newsletter and Schneier on Security blog have made him one of the most widely cited public communicators on cryptography and security policy since the 1990s.

title: Casey Ellis
summary: Casey Ellis is an Australian security researcher and entrepreneur who founded Bugcrowd in 2012, one of the first companies to commercialize crowdsourced bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, helping mainstream the practice across the cybersecurity industry.

title: Cesar Cerrudo
summary: Cesar Cerrudo is an Argentine security researcher known for early vulnerability research in Microsoft SQL Server and Windows, and for later work as CTO of IOActive Labs exposing widespread security weaknesses in traffic-control systems and other smart-city infrastructure.

title: Charlie Miller
summary: Charlie Miller is an American security researcher and former NSA analyst best known for being the first to remotely exploit the iPhone (2007), for four Pwn2Own competition wins, and for the 2015 remote hack of a Jeep Cherokee with Chris Valasek that triggered a 1.4-million-vehicle recall by Fiat Chrysler.

title: Chris Eagle
summary: Chris Eagle is a computer security researcher and long-time Computer Science faculty member at the Naval Postgraduate School, best known as the author of The IDA Pro Book, co-author of The Ghidra Book, creator of widely used IDA Pro reverse-engineering plugins, a member of DARPA's Cyber Grand Challenge Competition Framework Team, and a longtime DEF CON CTF organizer under the DDTEK banner.

title: Chris Valasek
summary: Chris Valasek is an American security researcher who, with longtime collaborator Charlie Miller, remotely hacked a moving Jeep Cherokee in 2015, a demonstration that triggered a 1.4-million-vehicle recall and helped establish automotive cybersecurity as a mainstream discipline.

title: Chris Wysopal
summary: Chris Wysopal, known by the handle 'Weld Pond' during his time with the hacker think tank L0pht Heavy Industries, was one of seven L0pht members who warned the U.S. Senate in 1998 that they could take down the internet in 30 minutes; he went on to co-found the security consultancy @stake and later the application-security testing company Veracode.

title: Clifford Stoll and 'The Cuckoo's Egg'
summary: The true story of how astronomer Clifford Stoll, tasked with finding a 75-cent accounting error, ended up tracking a KGB-sponsored hacker through the early internet.

title: Dafydd Stuttard
summary: Dafydd Stuttard is a British security researcher who built Burp Suite between 2003 and 2006, founded the company PortSwigger to develop it, and co-authored the standard reference text "The Web Application Hacker's Handbook."

title: Dan Kaminsky
summary: Dan Kaminsky was an American security researcher best known for discovering a fundamental 2008 flaw in the Domain Name System that enabled widespread cache poisoning, and for organizing an unprecedented coordinated, multi-vendor patch before public disclosure.

title: Dave Aitel
summary: Dave Aitel is an American computer security researcher and former NSA research scientist who founded Immunity, Inc. in 2002, building the commercial CANVAS exploitation framework and SPIKE fuzzing toolset, and who later became an influential voice in cybersecurity policy commentary.

title: David Litchfield
summary: David Litchfield is a British security researcher and co-founder of Next Generation Security Software (NGSSoftware), known for extensive Oracle Database and Microsoft SQL Server vulnerability research and for co-authoring "The Shellcoder's Handbook" and "The Database Hacker's Handbook."

title: Dino Dai Zovi
summary: Dino Dai Zovi is an American security researcher best known for exploiting a zero-day QuickTime/Safari vulnerability that produced the first-ever Pwn2Own win at CanSecWest 2007, for co-authoring 'The Mac Hacker's Handbook' and 'iOS Hacker's Handbook', and for co-founding the security firms Trail of Bits and Capsule8.

title: Edward Snowden
summary: Edward Snowden is a former CIA and NSA contractor who in June 2013 disclosed thousands of classified U.S. government documents revealing global mass-surveillance programs, triggering an international debate on privacy, security, and government transparency and leading to U.S. Espionage Act charges against him.

title: Elias Levy
summary: Elias Levy, using the handle 'Aleph One,' wrote the 1996 Phrack article 'Smashing The Stack For Fun And Profit,' the tutorial widely credited with popularizing stack-based buffer overflow exploitation, and for over five years moderated the Bugtraq mailing list at the center of the 1990s-2000s full-disclosure movement.

title: Eric Corley
summary: Eric Corley, known publicly by the pen name Emmanuel Goldstein, is an American publisher and broadcaster whose radio program, biennial HOPE hacker conference, and role as lead defendant in the DeCSS anti-circumvention lawsuit made him one of the most visible individual figures in American hacker culture from the 1980s onward.

title: Felix "FX" Lindner
summary: Felix "FX" Lindner was a German security researcher and founder of the Phenoelit hacking group, best known as a pioneer of Cisco IOS and embedded-router exploitation research, and later founder of the Berlin-based security firm Recurity Labs.

title: Frank Rieger
summary: Frank Rieger is a German hacker, entrepreneur, and longtime spokesperson for the Chaos Computer Club (CCC), best known for publicizing the CCC's 2013 defeat of Apple's Touch ID fingerprint sensor and for co-founding GSMK, maker of the secure CryptoPhone.

title: George 'geohot' Hotz: The iPhone Jailbreaker
summary: The story of George Hotz, the prodigious hacker who first carrier-unlocked the iPhone and later took on Sony's PlayStation 3.

title: Gordon Lyon
summary: Gordon Lyon, known by the handle 'Fyodor,' wrote and released the Nmap Security Scanner in 1997 and has remained its lead developer for nearly three decades, while also founding Insecure.Org, SecLists.Org, and SecTools.Org — long-running pieces of infrastructure that the security research community still relies on.

title: Halvar Flake
summary: Halvar Flake, the handle of German mathematician Thomas Dullien, pioneered graph-based binary diffing and reverse-engineering tooling through his company zynamics (acquired by Google in 2011), and later helped surface the Rowhammer hardware exploit and co-founded the profiling startup Optimyze (acquired by Elastic in 2021).

title: H. D. Moore
summary: H. D. Moore is a security researcher and entrepreneur best known for founding the Metasploit Project in 2003, which grew into the world's most widely used open-source penetration testing framework; he later led security research at Rapid7 and founded the network-discovery company that became runZero.

title: James Forshaw
summary: James Forshaw is a British computer security researcher on Google's Project Zero team renowned for deep Windows internals vulnerability research, a record-setting Microsoft bug bounty, competitive exploit wins at Pwn2Own, and authorship of widely used security textbooks on network protocols and Windows security.

title: James Kettle
summary: James Kettle, known online as 'albinowax', is a British web security researcher and Director of Research at PortSwigger (maker of Burp Suite), best known for reviving and popularizing HTTP request smuggling through his 2019 'HTTP Desync Attacks' research, alongside influential work on web cache poisoning and web race conditions.

title: Jan Krissler
summary: Jan Krissler, known by the handle 'Starbug', is a German security researcher and long-time Chaos Computer Club member whose public demonstrations against fingerprint and iris authentication systems — including defeating Apple's Touch ID days after its 2013 launch and reconstructing a German cabinet minister's fingerprint from photographs in 2014 — became landmark illustrations of the fragility of biometric security.

title: Jeff Moss
summary: Jeff Moss, known by the handle 'The Dark Tangent,' founded the DEF CON and Black Hat Briefings security conferences and later moved into institutional roles including ICANN Chief Security Officer and U.S. Department of Homeland Security Advisory Council member, becoming one of the clearest examples of a hacker-scene figure crossing into mainstream security and internet-governance institutions.

title: Jennifer Granick
summary: Jennifer Granick is an American attorney who began her career defending accused computer hackers in the 1990s and went on to become one of the United States' leading legal voices on digital civil liberties, directing Stanford Law School's Center for Internet and Society and holding senior counsel roles at the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the ACLU.

title: Jeremiah Grossman
summary: Jeremiah Grossman is an American computer security researcher who founded WhiteHat Security in 2001 after working as Yahoo!'s information security officer, becoming one of the earliest professional voices in cross-site scripting and web application security research and helping to institutionalize the field through the Web Application Security Consortium and the annual 'Top 10 Web Hacking Techniques' list.

title: Joanna Rutkowska
summary: Joanna Rutkowska is a Polish computer security researcher best known for the 2006 "Blue Pill" hardware-virtualization rootkit concept, for founding Invisible Things Lab, and for creating the security-by-isolation desktop operating system Qubes OS.

title: John Draper
summary: John Draper, known as 'Captain Crunch,' is a foundational figure of phone phreaking whose discovery that a cereal-box toy whistle reproduced AT&T's 2600 Hz control tone helped launch blue-box phreaking and, indirectly, informed the founding partnership between Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs.

title: Julian Assange
summary: A teenage Australian hacker turned publisher, Julian Assange went from breaching military and telecom networks under the handle 'Mendax' to founding WikiLeaks and becoming the central, polarizing figure in a decades-long legal battle over the boundaries of journalism, national security, and personal accountability.

title: Karsten Nohl
summary: Karsten Nohl is a German cryptographer and security researcher best known for cracking the GSM A5/1 cipher and the MIFARE Classic RFID card encryption, and for co-discovering the 2014 BadUSB firmware vulnerability; he leads Security Research Labs, a Berlin-based security research consultancy.

title: Katie Moussouris
summary: Katie Moussouris is an American security researcher and policy advocate who created Microsoft's first bug bounty program, helped design the U.S. Department of Defense's "Hack the Pentagon" pilot, and founded the vulnerability-disclosure consultancy Luta Security.

title: Kevin Mahaffey
summary: Kevin Mahaffey is a cybersecurity entrepreneur and researcher best known as co-founder and CTO of Lookout, the mobile security company, and for co-discovering critical remote-exploit vulnerabilities in the Tesla Model S alongside researcher Marc Rogers in 2015.

title: Kevin Mitnick: A Complete History
summary: From his Los Angeles childhood and early phone-phreaking to the 1990s manhunt, prison, and his later career as a renowned security consultant.

title: Kevin Poulsen
summary: Kevin Poulsen, known by the handle 'Dark Dante,' was a phone phreaker and hacker who rigged a 1990 radio-station phone contest to win a Porsche and later reinvented himself as an award-winning Wired News journalist who helped uncover Chelsea Manning as the source of the WikiLeaks military and diplomatic leaks.

title: Kymberlee Price
summary: Kymberlee Price is an American product security executive whose two-decade career at Microsoft, BlackBerry, Synack, Bugcrowd, and New Relic centers on building vulnerability coordination and bug bounty programs, including Microsoft's first security researcher outreach effort and the BlueHat conference she co-started in 2005.

title: Linus Torvalds
summary: Finnish-American software engineer who created the Linux kernel in 1991 and Git in 2005, becoming the central technical authority behind the dominant open-source operating system underlying most internet servers, Android devices, and much of the world's computing infrastructure.

title: Marc Maiffret
summary: Marc Maiffret is an American security researcher who, as a teenage former hacker, co-founded eEye Digital Security in 1998 and went on to discover and publicly analyze the 2001 Code Red worm, becoming an early and influential figure in commercial Windows/IIS vulnerability research.

title: Marcus Hutchins: The Accidental Hero of WannaCry
summary: The story of Marcus Hutchins, a young malware researcher who discovered the 'kill switch' that helped halt the global WannaCry ransomware attack.

title: Marcus Ranum
summary: Marcus J. Ranum is an American computer security researcher and engineer credited with designing some of the earliest commercial firewall systems and later founding a pioneering network intrusion-detection company, making him one of the formative figures in modern network perimeter security.

title: Marion Marschalek
summary: Marion Marschalek is an Austrian-born reverse engineer and malware analyst whose confirmed career spans Ikarus Security Software, Intel's STORM hardware-security team, and AWS GuardDuty, and who now runs her own reverse-engineering consultancy, Hack & Cheese, while remaining active in the BlackHoodie women-in-reverse-engineering community.

title: Michal Zalewski
summary: Polish-born security researcher known online as 'lcamtuf', a prolific Bugtraq-era vulnerability researcher whose passive-fingerprinting tool p0f, web-security books, and coverage-guided fuzzer American Fuzzy Lop (afl) reshaped both browser-security research and modern bug-finding practice.

title: Mikko Hyppönen
summary: Mikko Hyppönen is a Finnish computer security researcher who spent over three decades at F-Secure and its successor WithSecure, becoming one of the most publicly recognized voices in malware research and cybersecurity communication, known for tracking down early virus authors and for widely viewed talks on cybercrime.

title: Moxie Marlinspike
summary: Moxie Marlinspike is an American security researcher who exposed foundational weaknesses in SSL/TLS certificate trust with tools like sslsniff and SSLstrip, then went on to co-create the Signal Protocol, the end-to-end encryption system now used by Signal, WhatsApp, and other major messaging platforms.

title: Peiter "Mudge" Zatko
summary: Peiter "Mudge" Zatko is an American security researcher who rose to prominence as a leading member of the L0pht hacker collective in the 1990s, later ran cybersecurity programs at DARPA and held security leadership roles at Google, Stripe and Twitter, and in 2022 became internationally known as the whistleblower who accused Twitter of severe security and privacy failures before Congress, the SEC and the FTC.

title: Natalie Silvanovich
summary: Natalie Silvanovich is a security researcher on Google's Project Zero team known for pioneering research into 'interaction-less' (zero-click) vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and video-calling applications, most notably a 2019 study of iMessage that uncovered multiple remotely exploitable bugs requiring no user interaction.

title: Nate Cardozo
summary: Nate Cardozo is an American attorney who spent about six and a half years as a Senior Staff Attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where he worked on encryption policy, government surveillance oversight, and coders' rights, before moving into privacy roles at WhatsApp/Facebook and later Google.

title: Nicolas Waisman
summary: Nicolas "Nico" Waisman is an Argentine security researcher who spent over a decade at Immunity, Inc. — rising to Vice President of Latin America — where he built a reputation as a globally recognized heap-exploitation expert, later contributing to GitHub's Security Lab research team.

title: Orange Tsai
summary: Orange Tsai is a Taiwan-based web application security researcher and principal researcher at DEVCORE whose disclosures of Microsoft Exchange Server vulnerabilities in early 2021 became known as ProxyLogon, and whose repeated Pwn2Own 'Master of Pwn' titles and Pwnie Award wins have made him one of the most recognized application-security researchers in Asia.

title: Peter Van Eeckhoutte
summary: Peter Van Eeckhoutte is a Belgian security researcher and trainer who founded the Corelan Security Team in 2009 and authored the widely used Corelan Exploit Writing Tutorials, becoming a leading figure in Windows exploit-development education.

title: Rain Forest Puppy
summary: Rain Forest Puppy (rfp) was the pseudonym of a security researcher who published one of the earliest widely-read technical descriptions of SQL injection, built the Whisker web-vulnerability scanner, and proposed RFPolicy, an early formal framework for coordinating vulnerability disclosure with vendors.

title: Ralf-Philipp Weinmann
summary: Ralf-Philipp Weinmann is a German security researcher and cryptographer known for practical cryptanalysis of deployed ciphers (DECT, EMV/ISO 9796-2) and for pioneering research into cellular baseband firmware vulnerabilities; he co-authored the "iOS Hacker's Handbook" and co-founded the security firm Comsecuris.

title: Renaud Deraison
summary: Renaud Deraison is a French-born security researcher who created the Nessus vulnerability scanner as a lycée student in 1998 and went on to co-found Tenable Network Security in 2002, serving as the company's chief technology officer through its 2018 Nasdaq IPO before moving into advisory and board roles across the cybersecurity industry.

title: Richard Stallman, the GNU Project, and Free Software
summary: The story of how hacker Richard Stallman launched the Free Software Movement and the GNU Project, creating the philosophical and legal foundations for open source.

title: Robert Hansen
summary: Robert Hansen, known by the handle 'RSnake,' is a web application security researcher who built the influential ha.ckers.org security community and XSS Cheat Sheet, co-coined the term 'clickjacking' with Jeremiah Grossman in 2008, and created the Slowloris denial-of-service tool.

title: Robert Tappan Morris
summary: Robert Tappan Morris is an American computer scientist who, as a Cornell graduate student in 1988, released the first worm to spread widely across the early Internet and became the first person convicted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act; he later co-founded Viaweb and Y Combinator and is now a tenured MIT professor of computer science.

title: Roberto Preatoni
summary: Italian penetration tester and internet entrepreneur best known as the founder of Zone-H, the long-running website-defacement archive, and of WabiSabiLabi, an early online vulnerability marketplace; in November 2007 he was arrested in Milan as part of the wide-ranging Telecom Italia "Tiger Team" wiretapping and corporate-espionage investigation.

title: Ross Anderson
summary: Ross Anderson was a British computer scientist and Professor of Security Engineering at the University of Cambridge whose research on cryptography, banking and ATM fraud, and the economics of information security helped establish security engineering as a recognized academic discipline, and whose 2001 textbook 'Security Engineering' became a standard reference in the field.

title: Runa Sandvik
summary: Runa Sandvik is a Norwegian-American computer security researcher who moved from Tor Project development and smart-weapon hacking research into building digital-security programs for newsrooms, most notably as director of information security at The New York Times.

title: Samy Kamkar
summary: Samy Kamkar is an American privacy and security researcher best known for writing the 2005 'Samy' cross-site-scripting worm that infected over a million MySpace profiles in under 24 hours, resulting in a felony conviction, and for a subsequent career of high-profile open-hardware security research including SkyJack, KeySweeper, and wireless car/garage-door attacks.

title: Silvio Cesare
summary: Silvio Cesare is an Australian security researcher active since the early 1990s, known for Phrack articles on binary infection techniques, a Snort IDS-evasion discovery, and later academic work on malware classification at Deakin University; he now runs the Canberra security firm InfoSect.

title: Solar Designer
summary: Solar Designer (Alexander Peslyak) created the John the Ripper password cracker in 1996 and founded the Openwall Project, becoming one of the most influential figures in open-source Linux security hardening and exploitation research.

title: Tavis Ormandy
summary: Tavis Ormandy is a British computer security researcher and a founding member of Google Project Zero, known both for a long record of high-impact vulnerability discoveries (Sophos, Cloudflare's Cloudbleed, AMD's Zenbleed) and for a 2010 disclosure dispute with Microsoft that became a touchstone in debates over responsible versus full disclosure.

title: the Grugq
summary: The Grugq is a pseudonymous information-security researcher, reportedly of South African origin, best known for pioneering early anti-forensics research in the 2000s, later reported involvement as a broker of zero-day exploits, and an ongoing career as an influential public commentator on operational security (OPSEC) and cyber conflict.

title: Tsutomu Shimomura
summary: A computational physicist and security researcher at the San Diego Supercomputer Center, Shimomura became internationally known after a December 1994 attack on his own home systems led him to help the FBI track and arrest fugitive hacker Kevin Mitnick, a chase he later recounted in the book Takedown.

title: Window Snyder
summary: Window Snyder is a security engineer and executive who rose from the 1990s Boston hacker scene through @stake and Microsoft's Trustworthy Computing initiative to become one of the most senior women in security leadership, later holding chief security roles at Mozilla, Apple, Fastly, Intel, and Square/Block.

title: Zach Lanier
summary: Zach Lanier (handle @quine) is an application, mobile, and embedded-systems security researcher who co-authored the Android Hacker's Handbook and presented widely on Android permissions, IoT device flaws, and embedded-hardware reversing while working at Veracode, Intrepidus Group, Accuvant LABS, Duo Security, and Cylance.

title: Anonymous: From 4chan Pranksters to Global Hacktivists
summary: The evolution of Anonymous from a leaderless, chaotic meme culture on the 4chan imageboard to a globally recognized hacktivist collective.

title: The Chaos Computer Club (CCC)
summary: Europe's largest and one of the world's most influential associations of hackers, known for its public demonstrations of security flaws and its strong advocacy for government transparency and data privacy.

title: The Cult of the Dead Cow (cDc) and Hacktivism
summary: The influential hacker group known for its high-profile pranks, coining the term 'hacktivism', and releasing controversial but powerful tools like Back Orifice.

title: Cypherpunks
summary: The Cypherpunks were an informal collective and mailing list founded in 1992 by Eric Hughes, Timothy C. May, and John Gilmore to promote privacy through cryptography, whose members' code, essays, and debates shaped PGP adoption, the Crypto Wars, and the ideological groundwork for Bitcoin.

title: DEVCORE
summary: DEVCORE (戴夫寇爾) is a Taipei-based offensive-security firm founded in 2012 as Taiwan's first company to offer red-team exercises, whose research bench — not just Orange Tsai — has produced hundreds of CVEs, the ProxyLogon/ProxyShell Exchange Server disclosures, and repeated Pwn2Own titles.

title: HITCON (Hacks In Taiwan Conference)
summary: HITCON (Hacks In Taiwan Conference) is Taiwan's longest-running vendor-neutral hacker and security conference, held annually since 2005 by the island's hacker/security community. It has grown from a single-track gathering into a multi-track event covering research talks, CTF competitions, enterprise and CISO tracks, and cyber-range training.

title: Keen Security Lab
summary: Tencent Keen Security Lab is a China-based vulnerability research team best known for a series of published remote and physical attacks against Tesla, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Lexus vehicles, disclosed responsibly to manufacturers between 2016 and 2021.

title: L0pht Heavy Industries: Advising the Senate
summary: The story of the Boston-based hacker collective that testified before the U.S. Senate, famously claiming they could shut down the internet in 30 minutes.

title: Legion of Doom (LOD): The Masters of the Digital Universe
summary: The history of the Legion of Doom (LOD), one of the most technically proficient and influential hacker groups of the BBS era.

title: LulzSec
summary: LulzSec (Lulz Security) was a short-lived hacktivist collective active from May to June 2011, loosely linked to Anonymous, that carried out a rapid string of high-profile breaches and DDoS attacks against Sony, PBS, Fox, InfraGard, Arizona DPS, and others before publicly disbanding after 50 days.

title: Masters of Deception: The New York Hacker Wars
summary: The story of the Masters of Deception (MOD), a New York-based hacker group whose expertise in telephony and epic rivalry with the Legion of Doom (LOD) defined an era.

title: Phone Losers of America
summary: Phone Losers of America (PLA) is a long-running phone phreaking and prank-call community founded in 1994 by Brad Carter (also known online as RBCP) and a collaborator known as Zak (el_jefe), which grew from a photocopied hacking zine into an internet radio show and podcast still active today.

title: Project Zero
summary: Project Zero is a team of security researchers employed by Google, founded in 2014 to find and privately report zero-day vulnerabilities in any software, not just Google's own, under a public 90-day disclosure deadline.

title: ShadowCrew
summary: ShadowCrew was an online carding and identity-fraud forum active from 2002 to 2004 whose members traded stolen credit card data, forged documents, and hacking tutorials; it was dismantled in October 2004 by the U.S. Secret Service's Operation Firewall, which led to 19 federal indictments and later revealed that a top member, Albert Gonzalez, had been a cooperating government informant.

title: WikiLeaks & Julian Assange: Radical Transparency
summary: The rise and impact of WikiLeaks, the controversial platform founded by Julian Assange that published vast caches of secret information, changing the face of journalism and activism.

title: Aircrack-ng
summary: Aircrack-ng is a free, open-source command-line suite for assessing WiFi network security, covering monitoring, packet injection, capture-driver testing, and WEP/WPA-PSK key cracking; it descends from Christophe Devine's original Aircrack and has been maintained since 2006 by Thomas d'Otreppe de Bouvette and the Aircrack-ng team.

title: BloodHound
summary: BloodHound is an open-source tool that maps Active Directory environments as a graph rather than a list, exposing hidden privilege-escalation paths that took defenders and pentesters weeks to find manually and revealing them in minutes, which made it a staple of both red-team operations and enterprise AD defense.

title: Burp Suite
summary: Burp Suite is an intercepting-proxy-based web application security testing toolkit created by Dafydd Stuttard (aka 'PortSwigger'), which became the de facto industry-standard platform for manual and automated web penetration testing.

title: Cobalt Strike
summary: Cobalt Strike is a commercial adversary-simulation platform created by Raphael Mudge as a paid evolution of his open-source Armitage tool; now owned by Fortra, it is a mainstay of legitimate red-team engagements and, via cracked or misappropriated copies, one of the most widely abused post-exploitation frameworks among ransomware gangs and state-sponsored hacking groups.

title: Frida
summary: Frida is an open-source, JavaScript-scriptable dynamic instrumentation toolkit created by Norwegian developer Ole André Vadla Ravnås, which lets researchers inject code into running processes on the fly to hook functions and inspect behavior without source code, becoming a foundational tool in mobile app reverse engineering and bug bounty hunting.

title: Ghidra
summary: Ghidra is a free, open-source software reverse engineering framework created by the NSA's Research Directorate, used internally by the agency for years before its unprecedented public release in 2019; it broke the commercial monopoly on high-end disassembly and decompilation tooling by giving researchers worldwide a no-cost alternative to IDA Pro.

title: Hashcat
summary: Hashcat is the world's most widely used GPU-accelerated password recovery tool, created by Jens 'atom' Steube; by proving that consumer graphics cards could crack password hashes orders of magnitude faster than CPUs, it reshaped both offensive password auditing and defensive password-hashing practice.

title: IDA Pro
summary: IDA Pro is the commercial disassembler and decompiler created by Ilfak Guilfanov that became the de facto industry standard for reverse engineering and malware analysis for nearly three decades, shaping how professional researchers read compiled binaries until free alternatives like Ghidra emerged.

title: John the Ripper: The Timeless Password Cracker
summary: The story of John the Ripper, the fast, flexible, and iconic open-source password cracking tool created by Alexander Peslyak ('Solar Designer').

title: Kali Linux
summary: Kali Linux is a Debian-based, open-source Linux distribution built for penetration testing and security auditing, released in March 2013 as a ground-up rebuild of Offensive Security's earlier BackTrack Linux.

title: The Metasploit Framework: Democratizing Penetration Testing
summary: The evolution of the Metasploit Framework, from H. D. Moore's open-source project to a powerful platform that made exploit development and penetration testing accessible.

title: Mimikatz
summary: Mimikatz is an open-source Windows post-exploitation tool created by French programmer Benjamin Delpy that extracts plaintext passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets from system memory, becoming one of the most widely used credential-theft utilities in both legitimate penetration testing and real-world cyberattacks, including major ransomware outbreaks.

title: Nessus
summary: Nessus is a vulnerability scanner originally released in 1998 by Renaud Deraison as a free, open-source (GPL) security tool; it was folded into Tenable Network Security upon that company's founding in 2002 and switched to proprietary licensing in 2005, becoming one of the most widely deployed commercial vulnerability assessment products.

title: Nmap: The Network Mapper
summary: The story of Nmap, the essential open-source utility for network discovery and security auditing, created by Gordon 'Fyodor' Lyon.

title: radare2
summary: radare2 is a free, open-source, command-line-first reverse-engineering framework created by Sergi 'pancake' Alvarez, valued for turning binary disassembly, debugging, and forensic analysis into a fully scriptable, cross-platform toolchain that anyone can inspect, extend, and run without a commercial license.

title: Snort
summary: Snort is a free, open-source network intrusion detection and prevention system created by Martin Roesch in 1998, later commercialized through his company Sourcefire and acquired by Cisco Systems in 2013 for $2.7 billion; it remains one of the most widely deployed IDS/IPS engines in the world.

title: sqlmap
summary: sqlmap is an open-source command-line tool that automates the detection and exploitation of SQL injection vulnerabilities and the takeover of underlying database servers, originally created by Daniele Bellucci in 2006 and developed since by Bernardo Damele and Miroslav Stampar.

title: Volatility Framework
summary: The Volatility Framework is an open-source Python toolset for extracting forensic artifacts from volatile memory (RAM) dumps, used worldwide in incident response and malware analysis since its 2007 debut.

title: Wireshark: Sniffing the Wires
summary: How a project started by Gerald Combs, originally named Ethereal, became the world's foremost network protocol analyzer.

title: YARA
summary: YARA is an open-source, rule-based pattern-matching engine designed by Victor Manuel Alvarez at VirusTotal to help malware researchers identify and classify malware samples using textual and binary patterns.

title: EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144)
summary: EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) was a critical Windows SMBv1 remote-code-execution exploit reportedly developed by the NSA, publicly leaked by a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers in April 2017, and subsequently weaponized in the WannaCry and NotPetya attacks.

title: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160)
summary: A critical bug in OpenSSL's TLS heartbeat extension let remote attackers silently read up to 64KB of a server's process memory, exposing private keys and credentials across roughly 17% of the internet's secure servers before it was patched in April 2014.

title: KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack)
summary: KRACK is a set of vulnerabilities in the WPA2 Wi-Fi protocol's four-way handshake, disclosed in October 2017 by researcher Mathy Vanhoef, that let an attacker within radio range force reinstallation of an already-in-use encryption key to decrypt, replay, or inject traffic.

title: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228)
summary: Log4Shell was a critical remote-code-execution flaw in Apache Log4j 2, a Java logging library embedded in an enormous share of enterprise and cloud software, that let an attacker achieve full server compromise simply by getting a single crafted string logged.

title: Shellshock (CVE-2014-6271)
summary: Shellshock was a family of critical vulnerabilities in the GNU Bash shell, first disclosed on September 24, 2014, that allowed remote attackers to execute arbitrary code by embedding malicious commands in environment variables processed by Bash.

title: Spectre and Meltdown
summary: Spectre and Meltdown were two classes of speculative-execution side-channel vulnerabilities affecting virtually all modern CPUs, disclosed on January 3, 2018 after independent discovery by multiple research teams including Google Project Zero, Graz University of Technology, and Cyberus Technology.

title: Stagefright
summary: Stagefright was a family of critical remote-code-execution vulnerabilities in Android's libstagefright media library, discovered by Joshua Drake of Zimperium in 2015, that could be triggered by a single malicious MMS message on an estimated 950 million devices.

title: Equifax Data Breach
summary: In 2017, attackers exploited an unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability (CVE-2017-5638) to breach credit-reporting giant Equifax, exposing the personal data of roughly 147 million people and triggering record regulatory fines and a rare DOJ indictment of foreign state hackers.

title: The Morris Worm: The Internet's First Wake-Up Call
summary: In 1988, a Cornell graduate student unleashed the first major internet worm, accidentally crippling a significant portion of the early internet and leading to the first felony conviction under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

title: NotPetya
summary: In June 2017, destructive wiper malware disguised as ransomware spread worldwide after attackers compromised the update mechanism of the Ukrainian accounting software M.E.Doc, using EternalBlue and stolen credentials for rapid lateral movement; it caused billions of dollars in damage at firms including Maersk, Merck, and FedEx, and was later attributed by the US, UK, and Australian governments to Russia's GRU military intelligence.

title: SolarWinds / Sunburst Supply-Chain Attack
summary: Attackers compromised SolarWinds' software build process and inserted the SUNBURST backdoor into Orion network-monitoring updates, a compromise uncovered in December 2020 after FireEye disclosed its own breach, exposing numerous U.S. federal agencies and private companies to Russian government-linked intrusion.

title: Stuxnet: The World's First Digital Weapon
summary: The story of Stuxnet, a sophisticated computer worm that physically destroyed centrifuges in an Iranian nuclear facility, heralding a new era of digital warfare.

title: DEF CON: The World's Most Famous Hacker Con
summary: From a small gathering organized by Jeff Moss ('The Dark Tangent') to the world's largest and most iconic annual hacker convention in Las Vegas.

title: Ekoparty
summary: Ekoparty is an annual computer security conference held in Buenos Aires, Argentina, widely regarded as one of the most important hacking and information-security gatherings in Latin America, featuring talks, workshops, CTFs, lockpicking, and wardriving.

title: The Hacker Ethic: MIT's Tech Model Railroad Club
summary: How the term 'hack' and the foundational principles of the hacker ethic emerged from a student club at MIT dedicated to model trains.

title: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly
summary: The history of 2600, the iconic green-covered magazine that has served as a vital source of information and community for the hacker underground for decades.

title: Bugtraq
summary: Bugtraq was the seminal full-disclosure security mailing list, founded in 1993 by Scott Chasin and moderated for years by Elias Levy (Aleph One), that became the de facto public venue for publishing and debating software vulnerabilities before passing through SecurityFocus and Symantec ownership, going dark around 2020-2021, and being reported as independently relaunched in 2026.

title: Die Datenschleuder
summary: Die Datenschleuder ("the data slingshot") is the irregular German-language print magazine of the Chaos Computer Club, published continuously since 1984 and covering the technical and political dimensions of hacking, privacy, and surveillance.

title: Full Disclosure (mailing list)
summary: Full Disclosure was a public, lightly-moderated security mailing list founded in July 2002 by Len Rose and John Cartwright as an alternative to Bugtraq after Bugtraq's moderation tightened under SecurityFocus/Symantec ownership; Cartwright shut it down in March 2014 citing legal pressure, and it was relaunched days later by Fyodor as a community-run successor.

title: The Hacker Manifesto: 'The Conscience of a Hacker'
summary: An exploration of the seminal 1986 essay written by Loyd 'The Mentor' Blankenship, which became the philosophical soul of the hacker movement.

title: Hacking: The Art of Exploitation
summary: Hacking: The Art of Exploitation by Jon Erickson is a widely used security education text that teaches exploit development from first principles through C programming and assembly rather than as a catalog of ready-made tools, shipped with a bootable Linux LiveCD for hands-on practice.

title: Packet Storm Security
summary: Packet Storm Security is a long-running public archive of exploits, security advisories, whitepapers, and hacking tools launched in 1998, which has survived multiple ownership changes, a non-profit relaunch, and a 2020s rebrand to packetstorm.news.

title: Phrack Magazine: The Hacker's Ezine
summary: The legacy of Phrack, one of the longest-running and most influential hacker ezines, known for its deep technical articles and philosophical essays.

title: Uninformed
summary: Uninformed (uninformed.org) was a technical journal published from 2005 to 2008 covering exploitation techniques, reverse engineering, and low-level Windows security research, producing 10 volumes and 47 articles before going dormant.

title: The BBS & Warez Scene
summary: Modems, message boards, ANSI art, and the communities that formed the modern hacker internet.

title: Hackers in Popular Culture: Film & Documentaries
summary: How movies and documentaries like WarGames, Hackers, and The Social Network have shaped the public's perception of hacker culture — for better and for worse.

title: From Hacktivism to Bug Bounties
summary: Public-interest intrusions, disclosure debates, and the rise of coordinated vulnerability programs.

title: Early Phone Phreaking
summary: The roots of hacker culture in the era of analog telephony and tone signaling.

title: The Philosophy of Responsible Disclosure
summary: An exploration of Responsible Disclosure, the ethical framework guiding how security researchers report vulnerabilities to vendors.

title: Dan Guido
summary: Dan Guido is a security researcher and CEO of Trail of Bits, the New York cybersecurity firm he co-founded in 2012, known for data-driven exploit/mobile-threat research, co-founding the Empire Hacking meetup, and steering the firm into blockchain and DeFi security auditing.

title: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman
summary: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman co-authored the 1976 paper "New Directions in Cryptography," introducing public-key cryptography and the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and jointly received the 2015 ACM A.M. Turing Award for this work.

title: Ken Thompson
summary: Ken Thompson is an American computer scientist who co-created the Unix operating system with Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs, later co-designed the Go programming language at Google, and authored the seminal 1984 Turing Award lecture "Reflections on Trusting Trust," which exposed how a compiler could be backdoored to insert undetectable trojans into software.

title: Loïc Duflot
summary: French security researcher employed by France's DCSSI (later ANSSI) who, from 2006 onward, showed that x86 System Management Mode, ACPI, and PC chipset/firmware features could be abused to bypass operating-system and hypervisor security guarantees, first presenting this work publicly at CanSecWest 2006.

title: Philip Zimmermann
summary: Philip R. Zimmermann is the American computer scientist who created Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) in 1991, the first widely used public-key email encryption program, and who was the target of a three-year US federal criminal investigation for allegedly exporting munitions without a license after PGP spread internationally.

title: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman
summary: MIT researchers Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman publicly described the RSA public-key cryptosystem in 1977-1978, a foundational algorithm for secure communication and digital signatures that earned them the 2002 ACM Turing Award.

title: Steve Wozniak
summary: Steve Wozniak is an electronics engineer who, before co-founding Apple Computer with Steve Jobs, built and sold illegal "blue box" devices for phone phreaking in the early 1970s -- an episode both men later credited as a formative step toward Apple's creation.

title: Anand Prakash
summary: Anand Prakash is an Indian bug-bounty researcher and entrepreneur who became one of Facebook's, Twitter's, and Uber's top-ranked vulnerability hunters, then founded the security consultancy AppSecure and co-founded the cloud-security startup PingSafe, acquired by SentinelOne in 2024.

title: John McAfee
summary: John McAfee was a British-American computer programmer and businessman who founded McAfee Associates in 1987 and created VirusScan, one of the first commercially marketed antivirus products, before leaving the company in the 1990s and later becoming a controversial public figure through a 2012 fugitive episode connected to a murder investigation in Belize, two Libertarian Party presidential campaigns, and a U.S. tax-evasion prosecution that ended with his death in Spanish custody in 2021.

title: Katsunari Yoshioka
summary: Katsunari Yoshioka is a professor at Yokohama National University who co-created IoTPOT, an influential honeypot and sandbox system for capturing and analyzing Telnet-based IoT malware that documented the surge of insecure-device botnets preceding and paralleling the emergence of Mirai.

title: Phineas Fisher
summary: Phineas Fisher is the pseudonym of an unidentified hacktivist who breached the government-spyware makers Gamma Group/Gamma International (2014) and Hacking Team (2015), publishing hundreds of gigabytes of internal source code, emails, and client lists as an explicit protest against the commercial surveillance industry, and who later claimed a 2016 breach of Turkey's ruling AKP party. Fisher's real identity remains unconfirmed.

title: Shalev Hulio
summary: Shalev Hulio is an Israeli entrepreneur and former Israel Defense Forces search-and-rescue officer who co-founded NSO Group in 2010 and led development and commercialization of its Pegasus mobile spyware platform, resigning as CEO in 2022 after international reporting and a US blacklisting over its use against journalists, activists, and officials; he later founded the cybersecurity company Dream Security.

title: Simon Choi
summary: Simon Choi is a South Korean malware researcher who founded the volunteer research group IssueMakersLab in 2008 to track North Korean state-linked hacking, worked as a senior researcher at the antivirus firm Hauri, and founded the Cyber Warfare Intelligence Center.

title: Taylor Monahan
summary: Taylor Monahan, known online as "tayvano," co-founded MyEtherWallet in 2015, founded and led MyCrypto from 2018 to 2022, and became one of the most visible investigators of Ethereum wallet hacks and crypto-drain campaigns after joining MetaMask, where she later led security research.

title: Troy Hunt
summary: Troy Hunt is an Australian web security consultant and educator who created Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) in December 2013, a free breach-notification search service that has grown to index billions of compromised accounts and become a standard reference point for the public, industry, and governments checking exposure in data breaches.

title: Costin Raiu
summary: Costin Raiu is a Romanian malware researcher who led Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT) from 2010 to 2023, directing landmark investigations into Stuxnet, Duqu, the Equation Group, Moonlight Maze, Carbanak, and Lazarus/BlueNoroff.

title: Dmitri Alperovitch
summary: Dmitri Alperovitch is a threat-intelligence researcher and entrepreneur who co-founded CrowdStrike, led investigations into Operation Aurora, Night Dragon, and Shady RAT, and headed the team that attributed the 2016 Democratic National Committee breach to Russian intelligence services.

title: Gil Shwed
summary: Gil Shwed is an Israeli entrepreneur who invented and patented stateful inspection, co-founded Check Point Software Technologies in 1993 with Shlomo Kramer and Marius Nacht, and led the company as CEO for three decades before becoming its executive chairman.

title: Aaron Portnoy
summary: Aaron Portnoy is an American security researcher who led TippingPoint's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) bug-bounty program and directed the first several Pwn2Own hacking competitions, before co-founding the commercial zero-day research firm Exodus Intelligence in 2012.

title: Aaron Swartz
summary: Aaron Swartz (1986-2013) was an American computer programmer and internet activist who helped develop RSS and co-founded Reddit, later becoming a leading advocate for open access to information before dying by suicide while facing federal prosecution under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

title: Albert Gonzalez
summary: Albert Gonzalez is an American computer hacker and former Secret Service informant who masterminded a series of credit and debit card theft rings, including the breaches of TJX Companies and Heartland Payment Systems, that together compromised more than 170 million card accounts. He was sentenced in March 2010 to a total of 20 years in federal prison.

title: Alex Ionescu
summary: Alex Ionescu is a Romanian-Canadian security researcher and low-level systems programmer best known as a co-author of the Windows Internals book series, as the former lead kernel developer of the ReactOS project, and for his early public research into the Meltdown/Spectre CPU vulnerabilities.

title: Amichai Shulman
summary: Amichai Shulman is an Israeli computer security researcher and entrepreneur, best known as co-founder and longtime chief technology officer of Imperva, a data and application security company he helped found in 2002.

title: Andy Greenberg
summary: Andy Greenberg is a senior writer at Wired magazine covering cybersecurity, privacy, and hacker culture, and the author of Sandworm, an investigation into Russian state-linked hacking group Sandworm and the 2017 NotPetya cyberattack.

title: Barrett Lyon
summary: Barrett Lyon is an American Internet entrepreneur and security researcher best known for founding Prolexic Technologies, one of the first companies to offer large-scale commercial DDoS mitigation services, and for helping law enforcement identify a Russian extortion gang that used denial-of-service attacks against online businesses.

title: Ben Hawkes
summary: Ben Hawkes is a New Zealand computer security researcher who was a founding member of Google's Project Zero team in 2014 and later served as its manager until his resignation in May 2022.

title: Ben Laurie
summary: Ben Laurie is an English software engineer and cryptographer known for writing Apache-SSL, one of the earliest SSL implementations for the Apache HTTP Server, and for later co-creating Certificate Transparency at Google.

title: Brian Martin
summary: Brian Martin, widely known by the handle "Jericho," is a security researcher and former hacker best known as the longtime operator of attrition.org and as a co-founder of the Open Source Vulnerability Database (OSVDB) and DatalossDB.

title: Bruce Potter
summary: Bruce Potter is an American computer security researcher who founded The Shmoo Group, a collective of security, cryptography, and privacy professionals, and co-founded the ShmooCon hacker convention held annually in Washington, D.C. from 2005 to 2025.

title: Chelsea Manning
summary: Chelsea Manning is a former United States Army intelligence analyst who, in 2010, disclosed hundreds of thousands of classified military and diplomatic documents to WikiLeaks, resulting in a court-martial conviction and a 35-year prison sentence that was later commuted by President Barack Obama.

title: Chris Evans
summary: Chris Evans is a British computer security researcher who created the vsftpd FTP server, led Google's Chrome security team and its Chromium Vulnerability Reward Program, and in 2014 founded Google Project Zero, a team dedicated to finding zero-day vulnerabilities across all software.

title: Christopher James Hadnagy
summary: Christopher Hadnagy is an American information security consultant known for popularizing social engineering as a formal discipline within cybersecurity, founding the DEF CON Social Engineering Capture the Flag contest, and authoring several widely referenced books on the subject.

title: Cris Thomas
summary: Cris Thomas, known by the handle Space Rogue, is an American security researcher and a founding member of the hacker think tank L0pht Heavy Industries, best known for testifying before the US Senate in 1998 and for later work at @stake, Trustwave, Tenable, and IBM X-Force Red.

title: Dan Farmer
summary: Dan Farmer is an American computer security researcher and programmer known for co-creating the COPS and SATAN vulnerability scanners and, with Wietse Venema, The Coroner's Toolkit for post-incident digital forensics on Unix systems.

title: Daniel J. Bernstein
summary: Daniel J. Bernstein is an American mathematician, cryptologist, and computer scientist known for creating security-focused software such as qmail and djbdns, and for foundational cryptographic designs including Curve25519, Salsa20/ChaCha20, and Poly1305. He was the plaintiff in Bernstein v. United States, a landmark First Amendment case that established source code as protected speech and helped dismantle U.S. cryptography export controls.

title: David L. Smith
summary: David L. Smith is a former New Jersey computer programmer who admitted to creating and releasing the Melissa virus in March 1999, a fast-spreading Microsoft Word macro virus that overwhelmed email systems worldwide and caused an estimated $80 million in damage.

title: Eugene Kaspersky
summary: Eugene Kaspersky is a Russian cybersecurity entrepreneur who co-founded Kaspersky Lab in 1997 and has served as its CEO since 2007, building it from a small antivirus shop into one of the world's largest cybersecurity vendors.

title: Gary McKinnon
summary: Gary McKinnon is a Scottish computer systems administrator who, using the online alias "Solo," gained unauthorized access to 97 United States military and NASA computers between February 2001 and March 2002, and who subsequently fought a decade-long legal battle against extradition to the United States.

title: Gerardo Richarte
summary: Gerardo "Gera" Richarte is an Argentine security researcher and exploit developer who co-founded Core Security Technologies in 1996 and later co-founded the satellite company Satellogic, becoming one of the best-known figures in Argentina's cybersecurity scene.

title: Graham Cluley
summary: Graham Cluley is a British computer security researcher, blogger, and public speaker who spent over a decade as a senior technology consultant at Sophos and now runs the independent security blog grahamcluley.com and co-hosts the award-winning Smashing Security podcast.

title: Greg Hoglund
summary: Greg Hoglund (born Michael Gregory Hoglund) is an American computer security researcher and entrepreneur known for pioneering Windows rootkit research, co-authoring "Rootkits: Subverting the Windows Kernel," and founding the security firm HBGary.

title: Guang Gong
summary: Guang Gong is a Chinese security researcher and the lead of the Alpha Team (Alpha Lab) at Qihoo 360's Internet Security Center, known for record-setting Android and Chrome exploit chains submitted to Google's vulnerability reward programs.

title: Hector Monsegur
summary: Hector Xavier Monsegur, known online as "Sabu," was a founding member of the hacking group LulzSec who became a cooperating FBI informant after his June 2011 arrest, an arrangement that led to the identification and prosecution of several other LulzSec and Anonymous-affiliated hackers.

title: Ian Beer
summary: Ian Beer is a British security researcher on Google's Project Zero team, widely regarded as one of the most accomplished iOS vulnerability researchers, known for discovering and publicly detailing dozens of critical remote and zero-click exploits against Apple's operating systems.

title: Ivan Arce
summary: Ivan Arce is an Argentine security researcher who co-founded Core Security Technologies in Buenos Aires in 1996 and served as its Chief Technology Officer, later becoming Chief Research Officer and CTO at the French security firm Quarkslab.

title: Jake Davis
summary: Jake Davis, known online as Topiary, is a British hacktivist who served as the public spokesman and Twitter operator for the hacking group LulzSec before his arrest in the Shetland Islands in July 2011.

title: Jayson E. Street
summary: Jayson E. Street is an American security consultant and self-described "hacker, helper, and human" known for physical penetration testing of banks, government buildings, and other secured facilities, and for advocating an education-focused approach to red team engagements.

title: Jeremy Hammond
summary: Jeremy Hammond is an American computer hacker and anarchist activist from Chicago who founded the security site HackThisSite and later, working with Anonymous-affiliated hackers under the AntiSec banner, breached the private intelligence firm Stratfor in 2011, leaking millions of internal emails to WikiLeaks; he was sentenced in 2013 to the maximum 10 years in federal prison under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

title: Joe Grand
summary: Joe Grand, known by the handle Kingpin, is an American electrical engineer and hardware hacker who was a member of the Boston-based hacker collective L0pht Heavy Industries and later became a professional hardware security consultant, author, and television host.

title: Johnny Long
summary: Johnny Long is an American security researcher and author who popularized "Google hacking" and created the Google Hacking Database (GHDB), later founding the nonprofit Hackers for Charity.

title: Kim Zetter
summary: Kim Zetter is an American investigative journalist who has covered cybersecurity, hacking, and national security since 1999, best known as a longtime Wired senior reporter and as the author of "Countdown to Zero Day," a definitive account of the Stuxnet cyberweapon.

title: Lauri Love
summary: Lauri Love is a British-Finnish computer activist who was accused by United States authorities of hacking into US government computer systems, including the Army, NASA, the Federal Reserve, and the Missile Defense Agency, during 2012-2013, and who won a landmark 2018 UK High Court appeal blocking his extradition to the US.

title: Liang Chen
summary: Liang Chen is a Chinese security researcher and co-founder of Tencent Keen Security Lab (formerly Keen Team), known for leading its browser and mobile exploitation research and for repeated wins at Pwn2Own and Mobile Pwn2Own competitions.

title: Marco Grassi
summary: Marco Grassi is a security researcher known for mobile and desktop operating-system vulnerability research, including work at NowSecure and Tencent Keen Security Lab (Keen Team), and for repeated wins at the Pwn2Own hacking competition.

title: Mark Dowd
summary: Mark Dowd is an Australian application-security researcher and exploit developer, formerly a senior researcher at IBM's Internet Security Systems (ISS) X-Force, and co-founder of the boutique vulnerability-research firm Azimuth Security.

title: Mark Loveless
summary: Mark Loveless, widely known by the handle "Simple Nomad," is an American security researcher and longtime hacker-conference speaker who founded the Nomad Mobile Research Centre (NMRC) and later led vulnerability research for BindView's Razor team.

title: Mark Russinovich
summary: Mark Russinovich is a Spanish-born American software engineer, security researcher, and author who co-created the Sysinternals suite of Windows utilities and, in 2005, publicly exposed the Sony BMG copy-protection rootkit. He is currently the Chief Technology Officer of Microsoft Azure.

title: Markus Kuhn
summary: Markus Kuhn is a German-born computer scientist and Associate Professor at the University of Cambridge Department of Computer Science and Technology, known for foundational research on compromising emanations (TEMPEST-style electromagnetic eavesdropping), hardware tamper resistance, and multimedia/digital watermarking security.

title: Matt Blaze
summary: Matt Blaze is an American cryptographer and computer scientist known for discovering a critical 1994 protocol flaw in the U.S. government's Clipper Chip key-escrow system, and for subsequent research on wiretapping, electronic voting security, and mechanical lock security.

title: Matt Suiche
summary: Matt Suiche (Matthieu Suiche) is a French security researcher and entrepreneur known for his work in memory forensics, founder of MoonSols and Comae Technologies, and for his early public analysis of The Shadow Brokers leaks.

title: Max Vision
summary: Max Vision (born Max Ray Butler) is an American former computer security consultant turned cybercriminal who, under the alias "Iceman," built and operated the CardersMarket carding forum before being sentenced to 13 years in federal prison for wire fraud.

title: Michael Calce
summary: Michael Demon Calce, known online as MafiaBoy, is a Canadian security consultant and former computer hacker who, at age 15 in February 2000, launched a series of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks that knocked Yahoo!, eBay, Amazon, CNN, Dell, E*TRADE, and other major websites offline.

title: Mustafa Al-Bassam
summary: Mustafa Al-Bassam is an Iraqi-British computer security researcher who, as a teenager under the alias "tflow", was one of six core members of the hacktivist group LulzSec in 2011; he later became an academic and entrepreneur working on blockchain scalability, co-founding Chainspace and Celestia.

title: Nadav Zafrir
summary: Nadav Zafrir is a retired Israeli brigadier general who served as commander of Unit 8200, the Israel Defense Forces' signals-intelligence and cyber unit, before co-founding the cybersecurity venture-building firm Team8 in 2014 and later becoming CEO of Check Point Software Technologies in 2024.

title: Neel Mehta
summary: Neel Mehta is a security researcher on Google's security team credited as a co-discoverer of the Heartbleed vulnerability in OpenSSL in 2014, and in 2017 he identified code overlaps between an early WannaCry sample and malware attributed to the Lazarus Group, the first widely cited technical clue linking WannaCry to North Korea.

title: Nicole Perlroth
summary: Nicole Perlroth is an American journalist who spent roughly a decade as the lead cybersecurity, digital espionage, and sabotage reporter for The New York Times, and is the author of the 2021 book "This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race."

title: Nir Zuk
summary: Nir Zuk is an Israeli-American security engineer and entrepreneur who helped develop early stateful-inspection firewall technology at Check Point in the 1990s and later founded Palo Alto Networks in 2005, where he pioneered the next-generation firewall concept as the company's CTO.

title: Onel de Guzman
summary: Onel de Guzman is a Filipino former computer science student who, in 2000, wrote and released the ILOVEYOU worm, which spread to tens of millions of computers worldwide within days and became one of the most damaging malware outbreaks in history.

title: Parisa Tabriz
summary: Parisa Tabriz is an American computer security engineer and executive at Google, widely known by her self-adopted title "Security Princess," who rose from a security engineering role in 2007 to Vice President and General Manager of Google Chrome.

title: Paul Kocher
summary: Paul Kocher is an American cryptographer who founded Cryptography Research, Inc. and is best known for discovering timing attacks and (with colleagues) differential power analysis, two foundational side-channel attack techniques, as well as for co-discovering the Spectre CPU vulnerability in 2017-2018.

title: Pedram Amini
summary: Pedram Amini is a computer security researcher known for co-founding the Zero Day Initiative bug bounty program at TippingPoint and for creating the Sulley fuzzing framework and the PaiMei reverse-engineering framework.

title: Peter Szor
summary: Peter Szor (Hungarian: Peter Szor) was a Hungarian-American computer virus and antivirus researcher, entrepreneur, and author, best known for his book The Art of Computer Virus Research and Defense and for his long career designing antivirus detection technology at Symantec and, later, McAfee.

title: Rafal Wojtczuk
summary: Rafal Wojtczuk is a Polish computer security researcher known for pioneering work on Xen hypervisor and virtualization-escape vulnerabilities, and for earlier foundational research on Linux/BSD kernel exploitation and buffer-overflow exploitation techniques.

title: Rop Gonggrijp
summary: Rop Gonggrijp (born Robbert Valentijn Gonggrijp) is a Dutch hacker and entrepreneur who founded the hacker magazine Hack-Tic in 1989 and co-founded the Dutch internet provider XS4ALL in 1993. He later became known for exposing security flaws in electronic voting machines used in Dutch elections and for assisting WikiLeaks with the 2010 'Collateral Murder' video release.

title: Sergei Skorobogatov
summary: Sergei Skorobogatov is a Russian-born hardware security researcher based at the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory, known for pioneering optical fault-injection attacks on secure microcontrollers and for the 2012 discovery of a hidden backdoor in a military-grade Actel/Microsemi ProASIC3 FPGA.

title: Sergey Ulasen
summary: Sergey Ulasen is a Belarusian malware analyst who, while working at the Minsk-based antivirus firm VirusBlokAda, led the team that first identified the Stuxnet worm in June 2010, a discovery that exposed the world's first publicly documented cyberweapon aimed at industrial control systems.

title: Shlomo Kramer
summary: Shlomo Kramer is an Israeli information technology entrepreneur and investor who co-founded Check Point Software Technologies, Imperva (originally WebCohort), and Cato Networks, three companies central to the development of the commercial firewall, web application firewall, and secure access service edge (SASE) markets.

title: Steven Murdoch
summary: Steven J. Murdoch is a British computer scientist and Professor of Security Engineering at University College London, known for research on the Tor anonymity network and for exposing critical vulnerabilities in the UK's Chip and PIN (EMV) banking card system.

title: Sven Jaschan
summary: Sven Jaschan is a German computer programmer who, as a teenager, authored the Sasser and Netsky computer worms in 2004, causing widespread disruption to computers and networks around the world.

title: Theo de Raadt
summary: Theo de Raadt is a South African-born Canadian software engineer who co-founded the NetBSD project in 1993 and, after his expulsion from its core team, founded the OpenBSD operating system project in October 1995, which he has led ever since.

title: Thomas Drake
summary: Thomas Andrews Drake is a former senior executive at the U.S. National Security Agency who was prosecuted under the Espionage Act after disclosing information about NSA mismanagement, including the failed Trailblazer program, to a journalist; the government's case against him collapsed in 2011.

title: Travis Goodspeed
summary: Travis Goodspeed is an American reverse engineer and embedded-systems security researcher, best known for creating the GoodFET open-source JTAG/hardware-hacking tool and for co-editing the reverse-engineering journal PoC||GTFO.

title: Vesselin Bontchev
summary: Vesselin Bontchev is a Bulgarian computer virus researcher who directed the Laboratory of Computer Virology at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences and became one of the earliest and most detailed chroniclers of Bulgaria's prolific early-1990s virus-writing scene, including the pseudonymous virus author known as Dark Avenger.

title: Victor Gevers
summary: Victor Gevers is a Dutch security researcher and self-described ethical hacker who has been active since 1998, known for founding the GDI Foundation and co-founding the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD), through which he has reported thousands of exposed databases and critical software vulnerabilities.

title: Vladimir Leonidovich Levin
summary: Vladimir Levin is a Russian former biochemistry graduate and computer programmer convicted for orchestrating a scheme that fraudulently transferred approximately $10.7 million out of Citibank corporate accounts in 1994, in one of the earliest publicized international bank-network computer fraud cases.

title: Wen Xu
summary: Wen Xu, also known by the handle "Memeda," is a security researcher known for Android/Linux kernel exploitation work at Keen Team, competitive results at Pwn2Own and DEF CON CTF, and academic fuzzing research completed during his PhD at Georgia Tech.

title: Wietse Venema
summary: Wietse Venema is a Dutch-American computer scientist and physicist best known for creating TCP Wrapper and the Postfix mail transfer agent, and for co-developing the SATAN network security scanner and The Coroner's Toolkit forensic suite with Dan Farmer.

title: William Binney
summary: William Edward Binney is a former United States National Security Agency mathematician and crypanalyst who served as a Technical Director and co-developed the ThinThread signals-intelligence program before becoming one of the earliest and most prominent whistleblowers on NSA mass-surveillance practices, years before Edward Snowden.

title: angr
summary: angr is an open-source, Python-based binary analysis platform combining static and dynamic (symbolic execution) analysis techniques, developed by researchers at UC Santa Barbara's Computer Security Lab and Arizona State University's SEFCOM lab, with strong ties to the Shellphish CTF team.

title: Core Impact
summary: Core Impact is a commercial penetration-testing and exploitation framework originally developed by Core Security Technologies, a company founded in 1996 in Buenos Aires, Argentina, with the tool's flagship version first released in 2002.

title: Cuckoo Sandbox
summary: Cuckoo Sandbox is an open-source automated malware analysis system that executes suspicious files in isolated virtual environments and produces detailed reports on their behavior, including API calls, network traffic, and file system activity.

title: Impacket
summary: Impacket is an open-source collection of Python classes providing low-level, object-oriented access to network protocols such as SMB, MSRPC, NTLM, Kerberos, LDAP, and TDS, originally created by SecureAuth and now maintained by Fortra's Core Security.

title: Netcat
summary: Netcat is a command-line networking utility for reading and writing data across TCP or UDP network connections, originally released by a programmer using the pseudonym *Hobbit* in 1995 and widely nicknamed the "Swiss Army knife" of TCP/IP tools.

title: Nikto
summary: Nikto is an open-source command-line web server scanner, originally authored by Chris Sullo, that checks servers for thousands of potentially dangerous files, outdated software versions, and common misconfigurations.

title: OWASP ZAP
summary: OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy) is a free and open-source web application security scanner, originally forked from Paros Proxy and first released in 2010, that became one of the world's most widely used dynamic application security testing (DAST) tools.

title: PowerShell Empire
summary: PowerShell Empire is an open-source post-exploitation and command-and-control framework, originally built around pure PowerShell agents for Windows, that was later merged with the Python-based EmPyre project and, after the original project went dormant, revived and continued by the security firm BC Security.

title: Shodan
summary: Shodan is a search engine created by John Matherly that indexes internet-connected devices and services rather than web pages, allowing users to search by device type, software banner, geographic location, and open ports.

title: Suricata
summary: Suricata is a free and open-source network intrusion detection (IDS), intrusion prevention (IPS), and network security monitoring (NSM) engine developed by the Open Information Security Foundation (OISF) and its community.

title: tcpdump
summary: tcpdump is a command-line packet analyzer originally developed in 1988 at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory that captures and displays TCP/IP and other network traffic in real time, built on the libpcap capture library it also spawned.

title: theHarvester
summary: theHarvester is an open-source intelligence (OSINT) reconnaissance tool that gathers emails, subdomains, hostnames, employee names, and other public information about a target organization from search engines, DNS records, and other public sources. It was originally created by Christian Martorella of Edge-Security Research and is now bundled by default in Kali Linux.

title: w3af
summary: w3af (Web Application Attack and Audit Framework) is an open-source Python framework for identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities in web applications, created by Argentine security researcher Andres Riancho starting in 2007.

title: The Ashley Madison Breach
summary: In July 2015, a hacker group calling itself The Impact Team breached Avid Life Media, the parent company of the extramarital-affair dating site Ashley Madison, and later leaked tens of millions of users' personal data after the company refused to shut the site down.

title: The Bangladesh Bank Heist
summary: In February 2016, attackers used stolen SWIFT credentials to issue fraudulent transfer instructions from Bangladesh Bank's account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, attempting to steal nearly $1 billion and successfully diverting $101 million, of which $81 million was routed through casinos in the Philippines and never recovered.

title: The Colonial Pipeline Ransomware Attack
summary: In May 2021, the DarkSide ransomware-as-a-service group breached the IT network of Colonial Pipeline, the largest refined-products pipeline operator in the United States, prompting a precautionary six-day shutdown of fuel delivery to much of the U.S. Southeast and a $4.4 million ransom payment.

title: The MOVEit Breach
summary: In May and June 2023, the Russian-speaking extortion group Cl0p exploited a critical zero-day SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2023-34362) in Progress Software's MOVEit Transfer file-transfer tool, stealing data from thousands of downstream organizations in one of the largest single-vulnerability mass-exploitation campaigns in history.

title: Operation Aurora
summary: Operation Aurora was a sophisticated cyberespionage campaign conducted between mid-2009 and December 2009 against Google and at least thirty other major U.S. companies, exploiting an Internet Explorer zero-day to steal intellectual property and access source code repositories; its disclosure led Google to stop censoring search results in mainland China.

title: The RSA SecurID Breach
summary: In March 2011, RSA Security disclosed that intruders had breached its network through a spear-phishing campaign and stolen data tied to its SecurID two-factor authentication tokens, information that was later used in an attempted intrusion at defense contractor Lockheed Martin.

title: The Sony Pictures Hack
summary: In November 2014, a group calling itself Guardians of Peace breached Sony Pictures Entertainment, wiping systems and leaking terabytes of internal data; the U.S. government publicly attributed the attack to North Korea, tying it to Sony's planned release of the comedy film The Interview.

title: Target 2013 Data Breach
summary: Between November 27 and December 15, 2013, attackers used point-of-sale (BlackPOS/Kaptoxa) malware installed on Target Corporation's payment terminals to steal data from roughly 40 million credit and debit cards, later followed by disclosure that personal information of up to 70 million customers was also exposed.

title: The WannaCry Ransomware Attack
summary: WannaCry was a fast-spreading ransomware worm that struck in May 2017, using the leaked NSA-developed EternalBlue exploit to infect hundreds of thousands of Windows computers across roughly 150 countries in a matter of days.

title: The Yahoo Data Breaches
summary: Between 2013 and 2014, attackers linked to Russia's FSB intelligence service compromised the entirety of Yahoo's user account database, affecting all three billion accounts; Yahoo did not publicly disclose the intrusions until 2016 and 2017, making it one of the largest data breaches in history.

title: Black Hat Briefings
summary: Black Hat Briefings is an information security conference founded in 1997 by Jeff Moss as a more corporate and professional counterpart to his hacker convention DEF CON, bringing together researchers, vendors, and government agencies to discuss vulnerabilities and hacking techniques.

title: CanSecWest and the Founding of Pwn2Own
summary: CanSecWest, a Vancouver-based security conference organized by Dragos Ruiu, launched the Pwn2Own contest in April 2007, creating what became one of the world's most prominent live hacking competitions for browsers, operating systems, and devices.

title: Chaos Communication Camp
summary: The Chaos Communication Camp (CCCamp) is an international outdoor hacker gathering organized by the Chaos Computer Club (CCC), held roughly every four years in Germany since 1999.

title: The Founding of the DEF CON Capture the Flag Contest
summary: The DEF CON Capture the Flag (CTF) contest was first held in 1996 at DEF CON 4, growing out of informal hacking games at earlier DEF CONs into what became known as the premier hacking competition in the world.

title: HOPE (Hackers On Planet Earth)
summary: HOPE (Hackers On Planet Earth) is a hacker conference organized by 2600: The Hacker Quarterly, first held in 1994 in New York City and traditionally staged every two summers since.

title: Operation Sundevil
summary: Operation Sundevil was a nationwide crackdown coordinated by the United States Secret Service that culminated in raids across more than a dozen U.S. cities in May 1990, targeting bulletin board systems (BBSes) suspected of trading stolen credit card numbers, phone-phreaking tools, and pirated software.

title: The Founding of the RSA Conference
summary: The RSA Conference, now the world's largest information security industry gathering, began as a small, single-panel gathering convened by RSA Data Security in November 1991 to debate the U.S. government's proposed Digital Signature Standard.

title: ShmooCon
summary: ShmooCon was an annual American hacker convention organized by The Shmoo Group, held in the Washington, D.C. area from 2005 until its final edition in January 2025.

title: APT29 (Cozy Bear)
